Lesson Overview: Putting It All Together—Unit 5 Synthesis

Lesson Focus

Lesson 8: Putting It All Together—Unit 5 Synthesis

Unit 5 Primary Standards: MLA.CW.REV.01, MLA.CW.REV.02, MLA.CW.PUB.01, MLA.CW.PUB.02, MLA.CW.COM.01, MLA.CW.COM.02.

Supporting Standards: MLA.CW.COM.03, MLA.CW.WR.05, MLA.CW.WR.08.

What You Will Learn

  • Synthesize feedback, workshop, revision, publication, and presentation decisions.
  • Diagnose the highest-impact next step for an unfamiliar draft.
  • Defend editorial decisions with standards-based evidence.
  • Prepare for the Unit 5 Final Assessment.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 8 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task: Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.
TermMeaningExample
synthesisThe integration of several ideas or skills into a new, coherent understanding or product.The final portfolio combines drafting, feedback, revision, and presentation.
diagnosisA reasoned identification of the underlying cause of a writing problem.The writer traces reader confusion to a missing scene transition.
editorial judgmentA decision about what to revise, preserve, cut, or present based on purpose and evidence.The editor preserves the unusual ending because it serves the theme.
revision priorityA ranked change chosen for its likely effect on meaning and readers.Clarifying the central conflict comes before correcting commas.
feedback loopA cycle of drafting, response, revision, testing, and further response.The writer revises, asks a new reader, and evaluates the result.
transferThe application of a learned skill to a new situation.The writer applies pacing techniques from fiction to a memoir scene.
publication readinessThe condition of being complete, polished, accessible, ethical, and usable by the intended audience.Final checks confirm permissions, formatting, and accessibility.
defensibleSupported by clear reasons and relevant evidence.The selection is defensible because it demonstrates both range and growth.
constraintA limit or requirement that shapes a creative decision.A five-minute presentation limit determines the excerpt length.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each clue to the precise term. Choose Check, study any mismatch, and retry. This practice is ungraded.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Which decision shows strong editorial judgment?

A. Correct every punctuation mark before deciding whether the central conflict is understandable.

This gives local correctness priority over a larger meaning problem.

B. Diagnose the unclear conflict, revise it first, then proofread after the meaning is stable.

Correct. The decision ranks revision by its effect on meaning and readers.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 8 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: The Integrated Editorial Decision Cycle

1. Establish Purpose and Constraints

Before revising, name the intended audience, desired effect, genre expectations, publication format, and nonnegotiable constraints. A change is “better” only in relation to these goals.

2. Diagnose Before Editing

SymptomPossible diagnosisTest
Reader is boredWeak stakes, repetitive scene, or flat pacingAsk where attention dropped and why
Ending feels suddenMissing setup or compressed consequenceTrace promises planted earlier
Voice is unclearInconsistent diction, perspective, or distanceCompare key passages aloud

Pause and Choose: Diagnose the Revision Need

Readers understand every event but say the ending feels unearned. Which response best diagnoses the problem?

A. Correct punctuation throughout the draft before investigating the ending.
Weaker choice. Correctness may matter later, but it does not address missing setup or consequence. This begins at the lowest revision level while a structural problem remains.
B. Trace what the ending asks the reader to believe, then identify where that change should have been prepared earlier.
Stronger choice. This turns the symptom into a structural test. The writer can plant or strengthen evidence before polishing sentences.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

3. Revise in the Right Order

  1. Meaning and purpose: central effect, stakes, theme, ethical representation.
  2. Structure: order, pacing, development, transitions.
  3. Scene and sentence craft: imagery, dialogue, syntax, diction, sound.
  4. Correctness and format: grammar, mechanics, consistency, accessibility.

4. Test the Revision

Do not ask only, “Do you like it?” Ask targeted questions: What did you expect? Where did your interpretation change? Which detail shaped that conclusion? Then compare feedback to the intended effect.

Pause and Choose: Test Against Purpose

A revision makes a story faster, but it removes the quiet observation needed to show the narrator’s change. Which decision is strongest?

A. Restore or reshape the observation because pacing improvements are not successful if they block the central purpose.
Stronger choice. Revision is evaluated against intended effect, not one isolated trait. The writer can seek a concise version that preserves the necessary change.
B. Keep the faster version because shorter writing is always stronger.
Weaker choice. Brevity is a tool, not an absolute rule. A change that erases essential meaning fails even if it increases speed.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

5. Publish and Present Responsibly

  • Verify ownership, permissions, and privacy.
  • Match formatting to genre and platform.
  • Provide accessible headings, links, images, audio, and contrast.
  • Prepare a concise author statement grounded in exact craft evidence.

Decision Rule

Preserve what works. Revise what blocks purpose. Reject feedback that conflicts with evidence or goals—but explain why.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 8 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Integrated Editorial Cases

Example 1 — Revision Priority

Case: A story’s dialogue is polished, but readers do not understand why the protagonist risks entering a flooded tunnel.

  1. Purpose: create a believable high-stakes choice.
  2. Diagnosis: motivation is missing; dialogue polish is not the main problem.
  3. Priority: plant an earlier obligation connecting the protagonist to someone inside.
  4. Test: ask a new reader to explain the choice before reaching the tunnel scene.
  5. Polish only after motivation and structure work.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which revision priority best addresses the flooded-tunnel story’s central problem?

A. Polish the dialogue first because clean sentences make every scene easier to understand.
Weaker response. Dialogue polish does not repair the missing motivation that makes the central action unbelievable.
B. Plant an earlier obligation connecting the protagonist to someone inside the tunnel, then test whether a new reader can explain the high-stakes choice.
Stronger response. This priority diagnoses the structural need, adds causal evidence, and includes a reader test before sentence-level polishing.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Conflicting Feedback

Case: One reader asks for more explanation of a recurring moth image; another says the image is most powerful when unexplained.

  1. Locate agreement: both noticed the image, so it has salience—meaning it attracts attention.
  2. Return to purpose: the writer wants ambiguity, not confusion.
  3. Revise by strengthening the moth’s patterned appearances without adding a direct explanation.
  4. Test whether readers can identify its emotional association while offering different interpretations.
  5. Decision: preserve ambiguity but improve coherence.

Example 3 — Publication Constraint

Case: A spoken-word piece depends on pauses and vocal emphasis, but the publication platform accepts only text and images.

  1. Name the constraint: audio cannot carry the performance.
  2. Identify essential meaning: rhythm and hesitation shape the speaker’s conflict.
  3. Adapt with line breaks, spacing, punctuation, and a short performance note.
  4. Add an accessible text description if a visual rhythm map is included.
  5. Author statement: explain the adaptation without claiming text duplicates live performance.

Synthesis Frame

For any new case, write: Goal → Evidence → Diagnosis → Priority → Revision → Test → Publication check.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: A draft has beautiful imagery but an ending that contradicts the protagonist’s stated goal. Name the first revision priority and a test.

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: First repair the action-and-goal relationship at the ending. Then ask a reader to explain what the protagonist wants and whether the final choice follows from that goal before polishing imagery.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 8 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Putting It All Together: Unit 5 Synthesis

Purpose

Synthesize Unit 5 skills by moving one substantial work through a complete, documented publication process.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Use precise evidence from your own work and the source provided.

Source for Your Work

Synthesis role: You are the author, reviser, collaborator, editor, publisher, and presenter of one substantial creative work. Every decision must serve both artistic purpose and audience experience.

1. Plan Before You Work

DecisionYour Plan
Purpose and intended audienceState each clearly.
Most important craft or communication needName the need and evidence.
Success indicatorDescribe what an effective result will do for a reader.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger decision-making? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Focus on surface correctness and visual polish because a clean product proves the creative work is finished.
B. Balance meaningful revision, conventions, feedback decisions, format, ethics, presentation, and reflection so the final product communicates intentionally.

3. Apply the Lesson

Complete a publication dossier for one 700–1,000 word creative work or an equivalent poem/script. Include the polished work, feedback-and-revision record, copyediting check, format rationale, publication/accessibility plan, author-presentation excerpt, and a 300–400 word reflection.

4. Revise with Purpose

Complete a final three-level audit—development, organization, and language/presentation. Cite one consequential revision at each level and explain how the finished work better serves its purpose and audience.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your work applies the lesson skill to a specific creative product.
  • Your explanation identifies a decision and its effect on readers.
  • Your revision meaningfully improves the work, not only its appearance.
TOR Help

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Putting It All Together: Unit 5 Synthesis

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original work, and explain your decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: The Launch Decision

A student editorial team must publish its annual collection tomorrow. The strongest story has an unresolved permissions question. The most polished poem does not fit the collection’s theme. Two collaborators disagree about the order, and the author scheduled to present the work has practiced an outdated draft.

Publication synthesis coordinates revision, feedback, collaboration, format, digital responsibility, presentation, and quality control into one defensible process.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. Rank the team’s four problems from most urgent to least urgent and justify the order using audience, ethics, and publication quality.
  2. Explain how the team can preserve author ownership while still making a unified final product.

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which plan demonstrates responsible publication synthesis?

A. Fix whichever problem is quickest, publish on time, and explain any remaining errors afterward.
B. Resolve legal and ethical risks first, confirm the authoritative versions, address audience-facing quality, document decisions, and publish only after a final check.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Create a complete Unit 5 publication dossier for a polished original work or coordinated mini-collection.

  1. Editorial purpose: Define audience, purpose, format, and quality criteria.
  2. Revision record: Document feedback from at least two perspectives and justify adopt/adapt/decline decisions.
  3. Final publication: Present a polished 700–1,000 word work, equivalent multimodal piece, or three-piece mini-collection.
  4. Collaboration and ethics: Include roles, approvals, version record, attribution, permissions, privacy, and accessibility checks.
  5. Author presentation: Provide a 4–6 minute script with context, excerpt, craft reflection, and closing.

Add a 250–300 word editorial rationale explaining how at least five Unit 5 skills work together.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the audience should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Complete three final revisions: one content or structure change, one audience or format change, and one conventions or accessibility change. Explain the effect of each.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the work becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The creative work follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
